title: Capitulum 2 · Garum Pompēiānum (The Pompeii fish sauce) · English → Latin, then Latin × 2
summary: Vir Rōmānus, Part I, chapter 2 (125 AD, Porcellus is 4; level A1–A2). It is the year 125. Porcellus is four. Bucca has bad fish sauce and wants the best: Scaurus's fish sauce, from the town of Pompeii. But Bibulus knows something about Pompeii. Bucca, Porcellus and Bibulus make the trip. There they will find a clever man, and walls full of filthy words. Grammar: Cuius? Genitīvus · numerī I–X · quot?. Full cast; narrator Iulia (Rossana). Every line in English, then in Latin; then the whole chapter in Latin only, twice.

BUCCA.name: Bucca (Vir Rōmānus)
BUCCA.design: A huge, loud woman in her forties who runs a street cookshop in ancient Rome: booming, warm, raspy chest voice, bossy, quick and funny. Speaks English with a light Italian accent (never American).
BUCCA.sample: Sausages! Hot sausages! One coin! What do you want? Do you want food? The cabbages are good. Be quiet, Bibulus, I am talking!

PORC.name: Porcellus (Vir Rōmānus)
PORC.design: A cheeky, greedy, loud young man with a high, boyish, slightly nasal voice: bright, always excited, often with his mouth full. Speaks English with a light Italian accent (never American).
PORC.sample: I am the emperor! Marcus, am I bigger than you? I think about sausages. I always think. Give me the sausage, please! Oink!

MARCUS.name: Marcus (Vir Rōmānus)
MARCUS.design: A serious, calm, very polite young man with a light, clear, boyish voice: precise, gentle and thoughtful, old for his years. Speaks English with a light Italian accent (never American).
MARCUS.sample: I am reading. The book is about philosophy. A philosopher is a man who thinks, a man who looks for the truth. I will not ride without a reason.

BIBULUS.name: Bibulus (Vir Rōmānus)
BIBULUS.design: A lazy old drunk man in his sixties: hoarse, slow, slurred and sleepy, gravelly, deadpan. Speaks English with a light Italian accent (never American).
BIBULUS.sample: Mmmph. What is this? Water? I would rather die. I am the emperor of wine. Bucca, I want to tell you something... Nothing. I know nothing.

PRIMUS.name: Primus (Vir Rōmānus)
PRIMUS.design: A pompous, theatrical middle-aged man who thinks he is a great prophet: rich booming baritone, grand and dramatic. Speaks English with a light Italian accent (never American).
PRIMUS.sample: Look! A new star! Today on this hill a king is born! O king! O future emperor! Look, gold! All kings smell, woman. All of them.

SECUNDUS.name: Secundus (Vir Rōmānus)
SECUNDUS.design: A fat, practical, slightly whiny middle-aged man: nasal tenor voice, sceptical and dry. Speaks English with a light Italian accent (never American).
SECUNDUS.sample: Where? The sky is big, Primus. Where in the sky? Which of the two houses? It is the smell of cabbages. And of pigs. Surely not.

TERTIUS.name: Tertius (Vir Rōmānus)
TERTIUS.design: A tiny, very old man who is nearly deaf and nearly blind: thin, high, quavering, confused and sweet. Speaks English with a light Italian accent (never American).
TERTIUS.sample: What is it? Is it the moon? Oh! Who is hitting me? The wall is rude. Is the dog the king? Oh. Kind people. Where is the world?

MONK.name: Frater Ignotus (Vir Rōmānus)
MONK.design: A grumpy elderly English monk in a cold medieval monastery: dry, low, weary and deadpan, a sarcastic murmur. British English accent (never American).
MONK.sample: I am Brother Unknown. The year is eleven fifty. The monastery is cold. The ink is cold. My fingers are cold. The abbot says: write this book. I write.

SABIDIUS.name: Sabidius (Vir Rōmānus)
SABIDIUS.design: A lazy, smug, elderly Greek philosopher who is a useless slave: soft, slow, silky, superior and unbothered. Speaks English with a Greek accent (never American).
SABIDIUS.sample: You buy my body. You do not buy my mind. My mind is free. My mind does not cut cabbages. Work is patient. Work waits. I am a philosopher.

HADRIAN.name: Hadrian (Vir Rōmānus)
HADRIAN.design: A commanding Roman emperor in his fifties: deep, warm, authoritative, amused, a rich and slow voice. Speaks English with a light Italian accent (never American).
HADRIAN.sample: Hello, Marcus! This horse is yours. Ha! Listen to him! You are not Verus, Marcus. You are Verissimus! And who are you, little one?

PLAGOSUS.name: Plagosus (Vir Rōmānus)
PLAGOSUS.design: A small, bald, furious schoolmaster: sharp, barking, nasal, shouting and strict. Speaks English with a light Italian accent (never American).
PLAGOSUS.sample: A new pupil! What is your name? Do you know your letters? Not even A? In my school nobody laughs. In my school everybody learns. Or hurts.

PARROT.name: Psittacus (Vir Rōmānus)
PARROT.design: A shrill, squawky cartoon parrot: high, scratchy, screeching, fast, repeating words, very comic. Not American.
PARROT.sample: Hello! Hello! Stupid Bucca! Stupid Bucca! Emperor! Emperor! Sausage! Sausage! When do we get to Rome? When do we get to Rome?

MAN1.name: Romanus (Vir Rōmānus)
MAN1.design: A gruff working-class man in his forties from ancient Rome: rough, tired, impatient, deep. Speaks English with a light Italian accent (never American).
MAN1.sample: What do you want? Here nobody is born. Go away, or the dog comes! The best slaves! Buy, citizens! Dinner is three coins. Here you pay.

goat: A single billy goat bleating loudly, close up, "meh-eh-eh"

items.en: Vir Rōmānus. Chapter two: The Pompeii fish sauce.
Prologue: what will happen?

It is the year 125. Porcellus is four. Bucca has bad fish sauce and wants the best: Scaurus's fish sauce, from the town of Pompeii. But Bibulus knows something about Pompeii. Bucca, Porcellus and Bibulus make the trip. There they will find a clever man, and walls full of filthy words.
items.la: Annus est centēsimus vīcēsimus quīntus. Porcellus quattuor annōs habet. Bucca garum malum habet et garum optimum vult: garum Scaurī, ex oppidō Pompēiīs. Sed Bibulus aliquid dē Pompēiīs scit. Bucca, Porcellus et Bibulus iter faciunt. Ibi virum callidum invenient, et mūrōs plēnōs verbōrum foedōrum.

items.en: Grammar: the genitive (whose?), the numbers one to ten, and quot? (how many?).
items.la: Grammatica: genitīvus (cuius?), numerī ab ūnō ad decem, et quot?

items.en: Grammar.
Whose is this pig? The pig is Bucca's. Whose is this wine? The wine is Bibulus's. It is no longer Bibulus's wine: Bibulus drinks it. "Buccae" and "Bibulī" are the genitive: whose a thing is.
items.la: Cuius est hic porcus? Porcus est Buccae. Cuius est hoc vīnum? Vīnum est Bibulī. Iam nōn est vīnum Bibulī: Bibulus id bibit. "Buccae" et "Bibulī" sunt genitīvus: cuius rēs est.

items.en: The genitive often stands after the thing: "Scaurus's house", "Bucca's nose", "the smell of the pigs". The smell of the pigs is strong. The smell of Bibulus is stronger.
items.la: Genitīvus saepe post rem stat: "domus Scaurī", "nāsus Buccae", "odor porcōrum". Odor porcōrum est fortis. Odor Bibulī est fortior.

items.en: Numbers: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. Quot? = how many?
items.la: Numerī: ūnus, duo, trēs, quattuor, quīnque, sex, septem, octō, novem, decem. Quot? = quam multī?

items.en: "How many pigs are in the pig pen?" — "Seven." "How many pigs are in the cookshop?" — "Eight, if you count Bibulus."
items.la: "Quot porcī sunt in harā?" — "Septem." "Quot porcī sunt in popīnā?" — "Octō, sī Bibulum numerās."

Reading one: The best fish sauce.
Bucca tastes the fish sauce and makes a plan.
items.la: Bucca garum gustat et cōnsilium capit.

items.en: The year is 125. Porcellus is now four years old. Porcellus is a small, fat boy.
items.la: Annus est centēsimus vīcēsimus quīntus. Porcellus nunc quattuor annōs habet. Porcellus est puer parvus et crassus.

items.en: Porcellus's nose is red. Porcellus's voice is loud, like Bucca's voice.
items.la: Nāsus Porcellī est rubicundus. Vōx Porcellī est magna, sīcut vōx Buccae.

items.en: Porcellus's feet are always dirty.
In the cookshop Bucca tastes the fish sauce. She makes a sad face.
items.la: In popīnā Bucca garum gustat. Faciem trīstem facit.

items.en: This fish sauce is bad.
All fish sauce is bad. Fish sauce is a dead fish in a pot.
items.la: Omne garum est malum. Garum est piscis mortuus in ollā.

items.en: No! There is good fish sauce. In the world there is the best fish sauce: the fish sauce of Scaurus.
items.la: Minimē! Est garum bonum. In mundō est garum optimum: garum Scaurī.

items.en: Whose?
Scaurus's! Umbricius Scaurus's! The fish sauce of Scaurus is the fish sauce of kings. The fish sauce of the gods!
items.la: Scaurī! Umbriciī Scaurī! Garum Scaurī est garum rēgum. Garum deōrum!

items.en: The fish sauce of the gods! Where is it?
In the town of Pompeii. In Campania. Near the sea.
items.la: In oppidō Pompēiīs. In Campāniā. Prope mare.

items.en: In Pompeii? Bucca... Pompeii...
What, Bibulus?
Nothing. Nothing. Why do you ask me? I am Bibulus. I know nothing.
items.la: Nihil. Nihil. Cūr mē rogās? Ego sum Bibulus. Ego nihil sciō.

items.en: Bucca counts her money: one coin, two coins, three coins... ten coins.
items.la: Bucca pecūniam numerat: ūnus nummus, duo nummī, trēs nummī… decem nummī.

items.en: Ten coins are Bucca's money. All of Bucca's money.
items.la: Decem nummī sunt pecūnia Buccae. Tōta pecūnia Buccae.

items.en: Tomorrow we go. Me, Porcellus and Bibulus. Bibulus carries the sack.
items.la: Crās īmus. Ego, Porcellus et Bibulus. Bibulus saccum portat.

items.en: Why me?
Because you always sit. The sack always sits too. You are friends.
items.la: Quia tū semper sedēs. Saccus quoque semper sedet. Amīcī estis.

items.en: Excursus: Mount Vesuvius. True!
What happened at Pompeii in the year 79?
items.la: Quid Pompēiīs accidit annō septuāgēsimō nōnō?

items.en: This is true. Near Pompeii there is a mountain: Vesuvius. In the year 79 Mount Vesuvius burns.
items.la: Hoc est vērum. Prope Pompēiōs est mōns: Vesuvius. Annō septuāgēsimō nōnō mōns Vesuvius ārdet.

items.en: Fire and ash and stones fall from the sky. The towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum lie under the ash.
items.la: Ignis et cinis et saxa dē caelō cadunt. Oppida Pompēiī et Herculāneum sub cinere iacent.

items.en: Many people die. Among them is a learned man, Pliny the Elder, who wants to see the burning mountain closer.
items.la: Multī hominēs moriuntur. Inter eōs est vir doctus, Plīnius Maior, quī montem ārdentem propius vidēre vult.

items.en: This is a bad plan.
In the year 125 Pompeii has already lain under the ash for forty-six years. People know the place.
items.la: Annō centēsimō vīcēsimō quīntō Pompēiī iam quadrāgintā sex annōs sub cinere iacent. Hominēs locum sciunt.

items.en: Some dig and look for precious things: gold, silver, statues. Afterwards people forget the place.
items.la: Nōnnūllī fodiunt et rēs pretiōsās quaerunt: aurum, argentum, statuās. Posteā hominēs locum oblīvīscuntur.

items.en: In the year 1748 people start to dig again. Today you can visit Pompeii: houses, streets, shops and walls full of writing.
items.la: Annō mīllēsimō septingentēsimō quadrāgēsimō octāvō hominēs iterum fodere incipiunt. Hodiē Pompēiōs vīsere potes: domūs, viās, tabernās et mūrōs plēnōs litterārum.

items.en: And the fish sauce? This too is true: Aulus Umbricius Scaurus makes and sells fish sauce in Pompeii.
items.la: Et garum? Etiam hoc est vērum: Aulus Umbricius Scaurus garum Pompēiīs facit et vēndit.

items.en: In Scaurus's house there are pictures of jars, and on the jars it is written: "The best fish sauce of Scaurus".
items.la: In domō Scaurī sunt imāginēs urceōrum, et in urceīs scrīptum est: "Garum optimum Scaurī".

items.en: Scaurus is the king of fish sauce. The king of rotten fish.
items.la: Scaurus est rēx garī. Rēx piscium putridōrum.

items.en: Reading two: Pompeii.
The trip to Pompeii. Where is the town? And who is the man in the ditch?
items.la: Iter ad Pompēiōs. Ubi est oppidum? Et quis est vir in fossā?

items.en: After three days Bucca, Porcellus and Bibulus stand near Pompeii. In front of them there is no town.
items.la: Post trēs diēs Bucca, Porcellus et Bibulus prope Pompēiōs stant. Ante eōs nōn est oppidum.

items.en: In front of them is a hill of ash. The hill is big, grey, silent. There are grass and two goats there.
items.la: Ante eōs est collis cineris. Collis est magnus, griseus, tacitus. Ibi sunt herbae et caprae duae.

items.en: Where is the town?
Look, the town.
This is not a town. This is ash.
items.la: Hoc nōn est oppidum. Hoc est cinis.

items.en: In the year 79 there was a town. Now it is ash. I want to tell you this, Bucca. But you talk, talk, talk.
items.la: Annō septuāgēsimō nōnō erat oppidum. Nunc est cinis. Hoc tibi dīcere volō, Bucca. Sed tū loqueris, loqueris, loqueris.

items.en: Where is the fish sauce of the gods?
Under the ash, little one. With Scaurus.
Suddenly a man comes out of a ditch. The man is small and thin. The man's tunic is dirty.
items.la: Subitō ex fossā venit vir. Vir est parvus et macer. Tunica virī est sordida.

items.en: The man's eyes are quick. The man's name is Furius.
items.la: Oculī virī sunt celerēs. Nōmen virī est Fūrius.

items.en: Hello, friends! Are you looking for fish sauce? Scaurus's fish sauce?
items.la: Salvēte, amīcī! Garum quaeritis? Garum Scaurī?

items.en: Yes! How do you know?
Everybody is looking for Scaurus's fish sauce. I have Scaurus's fish sauce. Real fish sauce! Forty-six years under the ash.
items.la: Omnēs garum Scaurī quaerunt. Ego garum Scaurī habeō. Vērum garum! Quadrāgintā sex annōs sub cinere.

items.en: Old fish sauce is good fish sauce!
Furius shows a jar. On the jar it is written: "GARUM OF SCAURUS". The letters are new.
items.la: Fūrius urceum ostendit. In urceō est scrīptum: "GARVM SCAVRI". Litterae sunt novae.

items.en: The ink is wet.
The ink is wet.
It is... it is the dampness of the ash. The ash is damp.
items.la: Est… est ūmor cineris. Cinis est ūmidus.

items.en: How much does it cost?
Ten coins.
Ten! I have ten coins!
What a wonder! That is the price. The gods want it.
items.la: Quid mīrum! Hoc est pretium. Deī volunt.

items.en: The gods want it, or Furius wants it?
The gods and Furius are friends.
Furius leads them into the ditch. Under the earth is an old street. There are walls, shops, doors.
items.la: Fūrius eōs in fossam dūcit. Sub terrā est via antīqua. Sunt mūrī, tabernae, iānuae.

items.en: On the walls there are many letters: names, words, pictures.
items.la: In mūrīs sunt multae litterae: nōmina, verba, imāginēs.

items.en: What is this? And this? And this?
items.la: Quid est hoc? Et hoc? Et hoc?

items.en: These are verses. The people of Pompeii write on the walls. Everyone writes. Boys, women, neighbours, drunks.
items.la: Hī sunt versūs. Pompēiānī in mūrīs scrībunt. Omnēs scrībunt. Puerī, fēminae, vīcīnī, ēbriī.

items.en: What do the walls say?
Listen.
A real Latin text: Pompēiī, CIL IV 4957, 3146, 1904.
The walls of Pompeii speak. And they do not speak nicely.
items.la: Mūrī Pompēiānī loquuntur. Et nōn bene loquuntur.

items.en: Furius reads the verses on the walls and explains them. The first verse is on the wall of an inn: guests wet the bed, because there is no chamber pot in the bedroom.
items.la: Fūrius versūs in mūrīs legit et explicat. Prīmus versus est in mūrō dēversōriī: hospitēs in lectō mingunt, quia in cubiculō nūlla matella est.

items.en: A chamber pot is a small pot: at night you pee in it. The guests admit the blame, but they give a reason.
items.la: Matella est vās parvum: in eō nocte mingis. Hospitēs culpam fatentur, sed causam dant.

items.en: The second verse is short: "Secundus shits here." The third verse is about the wall itself: the wall is tired, because everybody writes on it.
items.la: Secundus versus est brevis: "Secundus hīc cacat." Tertius versus est dē mūrō ipsō: mūrus est fessus, quia omnēs in eō scrībunt.

items.en: The real text.
We wet the bed. I admit it, we did wrong, host.
items.la: Miximus in lecto. Fateor, peccavimus, hospes.

items.en: If you say: why? There was no chamber pot.
items.la: Si dices: quare? Nulla matella fuit.

items.en: Secundus shits here.
I wonder, o wall, that you have not fallen down in ruins,
items.la: Admiror, o paries, te non cecidisse ruinis,

items.en: you who hold up the boring stuff of so many writers.

Three real Pompeii wall writings, Corpus Inscriptionum Latinarum (CIL) volume IV. (1) CIL IV 4957, in an inn: "We pissed in the bed. I admit it, host, we did wrong. If you ask why: there was no chamber pot." It is a neat elegiac couplet. Poetry, about piss. (2) CIL IV 3146: "Secundus shits here." Rome's oldest status update. (3) CIL IV 1904 and copies: "I am amazed, O wall, that you have not fallen down in ruins, you who carry the boring scribbles of so many writers." Grammar to spot: genitive plural "scriptorum" (of writers), "tot" = so many, "te non cecidisse" = that you have not fallen (accusative + infinitive, coming later in this book).
Reading three: Furius's fish sauce.
Bucca buys the fish sauce. What is in the jar?
items.la: Bucca garum emit. Quid est in urceō?

items.en: "Secundus shits here"? Who is Secundus?
The astrologer! Secundus the astrologer!
Perhaps. Astrologers shit everywhere.
Porcellus finds a piece of charcoal on the ground. Porcellus wants to write on the wall. But Porcellus does not know his letters.
items.la: Porcellus carbōnem in terrā invenit. Porcellus in mūrō scrībere vult. Sed Porcellus litterās nōn scit.

items.en: Porcellus draws a pig. Porcellus's pig has four feet and a tail and a big nose.
items.la: Porcellus porcum pingit. Porcus Porcellī quattuor pedēs habet et caudam et nāsum magnum.

items.en: Under the pig Porcellus draws... something. Nobody knows what. Even today nobody knows.
items.la: Sub porcō Porcellus pingit… aliquid. Nēmō scit quid. Etiam hodiē nēmō scit.

items.en: Bucca gives the ten coins to Furius. Furius gives the jar to Bucca. Furius laughs. Furius runs.
items.la: Bucca decem nummōs Fūriō dat. Fūrius urceum Buccae dat. Fūrius cachinnat. Fūrius currit.

items.en: Furius is gone.
A kind man.
A quick man.
In the street Bucca opens the jar. Bucca tastes the fish sauce. Bucca's face changes.
items.la: In viā Bucca urceum aperit. Bucca garum gustat. Faciēs Buccae mūtātur.

items.en: First it is red. Then it is white. Then it is green.
items.la: Prīmum est rubra. Deinde est alba. Deinde est viridis.

items.en: Is it the fish sauce of the gods?
It is... sea water. And salt. And... one fish. One small fish. And the fish is alive!
items.la: Est… aqua marīna. Et sāl. Et… piscis ūnus. Ūnus parvus piscis. Et piscis vīvit!

items.en: The fish jumps out of the jar. Porcellus catches the fish. Porcellus kisses the fish.
items.la: Piscis ex urceō salit. Porcellus piscem capit. Porcellus piscem ōsculātur.

items.en: My friend!
Bucca, I want to tell you: Pompeii...
BE QUIET, BIBULUS!
They go back home. Bucca has no coins. Bibulus carries the sack: in the sack is Furius's jar.
items.la: Domum redeunt. Bucca nūllōs nummōs habet. Bibulus saccum portat: in saccō est urceus Fūriī.

items.en: Porcellus carries the fish. The fish is happy. The fish is the only one who is happy.
items.la: Porcellus piscem portat. Piscis est laetus. Piscis est sōlus laetus.

items.en: In front of the door of the big house sits little Marcus. Marcus too is four years old.
items.la: Ante iānuam domūs magnae sedet Marcus parvus. Marcus quoque quattuor annōs habet.

items.en: Marcus is reading a book. Marcus already reads, at four years old.
items.la: Marcus librum legit. Marcus iam legit, quattuor annōs nātus.

items.en: What are you doing?
I am reading. The book is about philosophy.
I have a fish.
Whose is the fish?
Mine! The fish of Porcellus!
The fish is not yours. The fish belongs to the sea. The fish is its own master.
items.la: Piscis nōn est tuus. Piscis est maris. Piscis est suī iūris.

items.en: Porcellus thinks for a long time. Porcellus takes Marcus's book and eats it.
items.la: Porcellus diū cōgitat. Porcellus librum Marcī capit et edit.

items.en: In the margin: Brother Unknown.
Brother Unknown on walls and on margins.
items.la: Frāter Ignōtus dē mūrīs et dē marginibus.

items.en: I, Brother Unknown, have read this chapter. The walls of Pompeii are disgusting. But we monks also write in books, in the margins.
items.la: Ego, Frāter Ignōtus, hoc capitulum lēgī. Mūrī Pompēiānī sunt foedī. Sed et nōs, mōnachī, in librīs scrībimus, in marginibus.

items.en: Brother Walter writes: "Oh, my hand." Brother Hugh writes: "This ink is bad." I write nothing.
items.la: Frāter Gualterus scrībit: "Ō, manus mea." Frāter Hugō scrībit: "Hoc ātrāmentum est malum." Ego nihil scrībō.

items.en: I am a good monk.
An old saying of scribes, at the end of a book: "Here ends the whole thing; for Christ's sake, give me a drink." That is: the book is finished; for Christ's sake, give me something to drink.
items.la: Vetus verbum scrīptōrum, in fīne librī: "Explicit hoc tōtum; prō Chrīstō dā mihi pōtum." Id est: liber est fīnītus; prō Chrīstō, dā mihi aliquid ad bibendum.

items.en: I love this saying. Bibulus loves this saying too.
items.la: Hoc verbum amō. Bibulus quoque hoc verbum amat.

items.en: Epilogue: what happened?

Bucca wanted Scaurus's fish sauce. So she went to Pompeii with Porcellus and Bibulus. But they did not find the town: only ash. Fūrius came out of a ditch and sold a jar. Under the ground they read filthy verses on the walls.
items.la: Bucca garum Scaurī voluit. Itaque cum Porcellō et Bibulō Pompēiōs iit. Sed oppidum nōn invēnērunt: tantum cinerem. Fūrius ex fossā vēnit et urceum vēndidit. Sub terrā versūs foedōs in mūrīs lēgērunt.

items.en: Porcellus painted a pig on the wall. Bucca paid ten coins, and in the jar there were water, salt and a live fish. In Rome, in front of the big house, Porcellus ate Marcus's book.
items.la: Porcellus porcum in mūrō pīnxit. Bucca decem nummōs dedit, et in urceō erant aqua, sāl et piscis vīvus. Rōmae, ante domum magnam, Porcellus librum Marcī ēdit.

items.en: What next?
Porcellus now has a fish for a friend and a book in his belly. Soon Porcellus will see a beautiful horse, and the emperor himself. And the emperor will give him a new name. Not a good name.
items.la: Porcellus nunc piscem amīcum habet et librum in ventre. Mox Porcellus equum pulchrum vidēbit, et imperātōrem ipsum. Et imperātor eī nōmen novum dabit. Nōmen nōn bonum.
